chapters.title: Thermodynamic foundations
chapters.what: A thermodynamic system is described by state variables (P, v, T) linked by an equation of state. Temperature is what equalises when bodies touch (the zeroth law).
chapters.looks: Isotherms on the P–v plane (2D) and the whole P–v–T surface (3D).
chapters.change: Cool a real gas below its critical temperature: the isotherm develops a flat liquid–vapour plateau.
chapters.use: Gas storage, engines, meteorology, chemical plants.
misc: Temperature and heat are different things.
The ideal-gas law fails near condensation.

examples.title: The ideal-gas law: one mole at 0 °C in 22.414 L
examples.world: Standard molar volume: P = RT/V = 101.3 kPa.

examples.title: Andrews' carbon dioxide isotherms
examples.world: Andrews (1869) found the critical point of CO₂: above it no liquid forms, however high the pressure.

examples.title: The critical point: Z_c = 3/8 for van der Waals
examples.world: Real gases have Z_c ≈ 0.23–0.31; the model's 0.375 shows its limits.

examples.title: The zeroth law: two blocks reach one temperature
examples.world: A thermometer works because it comes to equilibrium with what it touches.

examples.title: Temperature scales: −40 °C = −40 °F
examples.world: F = 9/5 C + 32; the kelvin is defined through the Boltzmann constant (SI 2019).

chapters.title: Properties of substances
chapters.what: Pure substances exist as solid, liquid and vapour; saturation curves, specific heats, expansion coefficients and the compressibility factor summarise their behaviour.
chapters.looks: Reduced van der Waals isotherms with the equal-area plateau; the whole surface in 3D.
chapters.change: Raise T_r through 1: the liquid and vapour volumes merge at the critical point.
chapters.use: Boilers and refrigerants, pressure cookers, rail and bridge expansion joints.
misc: Water boils below 100 °C on a mountain.
The van der Waals loop inside the dome is unphysical — Maxwell's construction replaces it.

examples.title: Liquid–vapour coexistence by Maxwell's equal areas
examples.world: At T = 0.9 T_c the gas condenses at a fixed saturation pressure.

examples.title: Supercritical: no boiling at all
examples.world: Supercritical CO₂ is used to decaffeinate coffee.

examples.title: Water boils at 90 °C at 70 kPa
examples.world: Clausius–Clapeyron with ΔH = 40.65 kJ/mol: why pressure cookers exist.

examples.title: Thermal expansion of a 100 m rail
examples.world: Steel (α = 12 × 10⁻⁶/K) over a 40 K swing grows 48 mm.

examples.title: Far from the critical point, gases are ideal
examples.world: At large volume Z → 1.

chapters.title: The first law of thermodynamics
chapters.what: Energy is conserved: the change of internal energy equals heat in minus work out. Work is the area under a P–v path; heat flows through resistances.
chapters.looks: A cycle on P–v enclosing the net work; a wall's temperature profile dropping across each layer.
chapters.change: Add insulation: the flux falls and most of the temperature drop moves into the insulation.
chapters.use: Engines, compressors, building energy, cooling of electronics.
misc: Work and heat are path functions; U is a state function.
A cycle returns U to its start, so net heat = net work.

examples.title: Net work of an Otto cycle = heat in − heat out
examples.world: Every petrol engine converts part of the fuel's heat into work.

examples.title: Isothermal compression work: RT ln 2
examples.world: Halving the volume of one mole at 300 K costs 1.73 kJ.

examples.title: Heat loss through an insulated wall
examples.world: Brick–insulation–brick: the U-value decides the heating bill.

examples.title: Energy balance of two blocks
examples.world: C₁ΔT₁ + C₂ΔT₂ = 0: heat lost = heat gained.

examples.title: Newton cooling from a lumped energy balance
examples.world: m c dT/dt = −hA(T − T∞) gives an exponential.

chapters.title: The second law: entropy
chapters.what: Heat flows by itself only from hot to cold; entropy of an isolated system never decreases. No engine can beat the Carnot efficiency 1 − T_C/T_H.
chapters.looks: Temperatures converging while total entropy rises (2D); the T–s rectangle of the Carnot cycle.
chapters.change: Narrow the temperature gap: less entropy is generated, and a refrigerator's COP soars.
chapters.use: Power plants, refrigerators and heat pumps, the limits of every energy technology.
misc: Entropy of one part can fall — the total cannot.
A perfect heat engine (η = 1) is impossible.

examples.title: Entropy generated when two blocks touch
examples.world: Any real heat transfer across a finite ΔT is irreversible.

examples.title: The Carnot efficiency
examples.world: Between 1800 K and 300 K no engine can exceed 83%.

examples.title: A refrigerator's best COP
examples.world: Freezer at −18 °C (255 K) in a 27 °C kitchen: COP ≤ 5.67.

examples.title: Stirling with a regenerator reaches Carnot
examples.world: Stirling engines in solar dishes and submarines.

examples.title: Heat always flows downhill
examples.world: A hot coffee in a cold room: the reverse never happens.

chapters.title: Thermodynamic cycles
chapters.what: Engines and refrigerators repeat cycles of compression, heating, expansion and cooling. The air-standard Otto, Diesel and Brayton cycles model petrol engines, diesels and gas turbines.
chapters.looks: The cycle on the P–v plane with the T–s inset (2D), and lifted onto the ideal-gas surface P = RT/v (3D).
chapters.change: Raise the compression ratio: efficiency rises, but real engines knock.
chapters.use: Cars, trucks, jet engines, power stations.
misc: Air-standard efficiencies overestimate real ones.
Diesel engines win by running at higher r, not by the cycle itself.

examples.title: Diesel: r = 18, cut-off 2
examples.world: Compression ignition allows high compression.

examples.title: Brayton: a gas turbine at pressure ratio 10
examples.world: Jet engines and power-station turbines: η = 48%.

examples.title: Real fuel–air mixtures: γ = 1.3
examples.world: The same Otto engine drops to 48%.

examples.title: Carnot between 1800 K and 300 K
examples.world: The upper bound all the others fall short of.

chapters.title: Fluid properties
chapters.what: Density, viscosity and the Reynolds number Re = VD/ν (inertia against viscosity) decide how a fluid behaves: creeping, laminar or turbulent.
chapters.looks: Drag coefficient against Re on log axes; Stokes streamlines round a sphere in 3D.
chapters.change: Raise the viscosity 1000×: the same flow becomes creeping.
chapters.use: Viscometers, sediment and dust, blood flow, lubrication.
misc: Viscosity is not density: honey is viscous, mercury is dense.
Stokes' law holds only for Re ≪ 1.

examples.title: Millikan's oil drops settle by Stokes' law
examples.world: A 2 µm oil drop falls at 0.11 mm/s — Millikan timed this to weigh the drop.

examples.title: A falling-ball viscometer in glycerol
examples.world: A 2 mm steel ball falls at 1 cm/s; the speed measures μ.

examples.title: Water in a 5 cm pipe at 1 m/s is turbulent
examples.world: Re = 50 000, far above Reynolds' critical ~2300.

examples.title: Blood in the aorta is (mostly) laminar
The boundary layer on a plate: 8.7 mm after 1 m
examples.world: Air at 5 m/s.

chapters.title: Fluid kinematics
chapters.what: A flow is a velocity field. Streamlines are tangent to it; particles follow pathlines; divergence is volume change and curl is local spin.
chapters.looks: Streamlines of ψ over pressure colour (2D) and the pressure-coefficient surface (3D).
chapters.change: Make the flow unsteady: streamlines and pathlines no longer coincide.
chapters.use: Aerodynamics, pipe networks, weather maps, blood flow.
misc: Streamlines never cross in a steady flow.
Irrotational does not mean still.

examples.title: Flow round a cylinder: C_p = −3 at the top
examples.world: The ideal speed doubles over the top of a cylinder.

expect.label: C_p at the top of the cylinder

examples.title: Stagnation-point flow
examples.world: u = x, v = −y: flow hitting a wall (nose of a car).

examples.title: The Rankine half-body
examples.world: A source in a uniform stream: the shape of a bridge pier.

examples.title: Unsteady flow: pathlines differ from streamlines
examples.world: Smoke from a chimney in a changing wind.

examples.title: A free vortex is irrotational
examples.world: Whirlpools and tornado outskirts.

chapters.title: Conservation laws for fluids
chapters.what: Mass, momentum and energy are conserved in every control volume: ρAV is constant along a pipe, forces balance momentum fluxes, and mechanical energy is traded between pressure, speed and height.
chapters.looks: A venturi coloured by pressure with manometer columns (2D); the axisymmetric duct (3D).
chapters.change: Narrow the throat: the speed rises as 1/D² and the pressure falls.
chapters.use: Flow meters, nozzles, jet thrust, pipe networks.
misc: Continuity alone fixes the velocity ratio.
Friction losses need the momentum or energy balance, not continuity.

examples.title: Continuity: halving the diameter quadruples the speed
examples.world: Venturi 100 → 50 mm: 2 m/s becomes 8 m/s.

examples.title: The energy balance: a 30 kPa drop
examples.world: ½ρ(V₂² − V₁²) = 30 kPa — a venturi flow meter reads this.

examples.title: Momentum and friction: pipe pressure drop
examples.world: 100 m of 5 cm steel pipe at 1 m/s loses 24 kPa.

examples.title: Incompressible flows are divergence-free
examples.world: The plane rotation-plus-strain field keeps area.

chapters.title: Internal flow
chapters.what: Flow in pipes is laminar (a parabola, f = 64/Re) below Re ≈ 2300 and turbulent above (flatter profile, f from Colebrook/Moody).
chapters.looks: The velocity profile across the pipe with the Moody chart inset (2D); the profile as a surface inside the pipe (3D).
chapters.change: Increase V: the profile flattens when the flow turns turbulent, and the friction factor jumps.
chapters.use: Water mains, oil pipelines, HVAC ducts, arteries.
misc: Laminar centre-line speed is twice the mean.
Roughness matters only in turbulent flow.

examples.title: Laminar flow: a parabola, u_max = 2V
examples.world: Oil in a narrow tube at Re = 500.

examples.title: Turbulent flow in commercial steel
examples.world: Colebrook at Re = 5 × 10⁴, ε/D = 9 × 10⁻⁴: f = 0.0237.

examples.title: Blood in the aorta
examples.world: A laminar, nearly parabolic profile in the large arteries.

examples.title: A water main
examples.world: 30 cm main at 1.5 m/s over 1 km.

chapters.title: External flow: drag, lift, boundary layers
chapters.what: Bodies in a stream feel drag (friction plus pressure) and, with asymmetry or spin, lift. A thin boundary layer carries all the viscous effects near the surface.
chapters.looks: C_D against Re with the Stokes line (2D); creeping-flow streamlines round a sphere (3D).
chapters.change: Grow the sphere from dust to a raindrop: Re sweeps from 10⁻² to 10³ and C_D flattens.
chapters.use: Vehicles, sports balls, sedimentation, spray drying, meteorology.
misc: Doubling speed quadruples drag (at constant C_D).
Terminal speed is reached when drag equals weight.

examples.title: A 2 mm raindrop falls at about 6.7 m/s
examples.world: Gunn & Kinzer measured 6.5 m/s; a rigid-sphere correlation gives 6.7.

examples.title: Dust settles by Stokes' law
examples.world: A 20 µm particle falls at about 3 cm/s.

examples.title: Laminar boundary layer on a plate
examples.world: Wind-tunnel models and aircraft skins.

examples.title: Lift from circulation (Kutta–Joukowski)
examples.world: Every wing's lift is ρUΓ per unit span.

examples.title: A spinning ball (Magnus)
examples.world: Top-spin tennis balls dip, back-spin golf balls climb.

chapters.title: Constitutive relations
chapters.what: A constitutive law links stress to strain for a material: linear elastic (Hooke), elastic–plastic with a yield point, or viscoelastic with time dependence.
chapters.looks: Stress–strain curves with yield (2D); a deforming block (3D).
chapters.change: Push past yield: strain grows much faster for the same extra stress.
chapters.use: Choosing materials, finite-element models, polymers and biological tissue.
misc: Elastic means it springs back, not that it is soft.
Yield is not fracture.

examples.title: Steel past its yield point
examples.world: Above 250 MPa structural steel deforms permanently.

examples.title: Viscoelastic creep (Kelvin–Voigt)
examples.world: Polymers and tendons keep stretching under a constant load.

examples.world: E ≈ 5 MPa, 40 000 times softer than steel.
